This is the portion of the meeting set aside for general public comment directly related to City business, for matters that do 
not appear on this evening’s agenda. If you are here for a specific agenda item that is under Unfinished Business or New 
Business, please wait until we reach that item. Items under First Reading & Referral will be discussed when they return 
under Unfinished Business, and we will hear public comment at that time.  Public comment requires a person to state your 
name and whether you are a resident of Bangor. The City Council has adopted a Public Comment Policy that we will 
adhere to. Statements during public comment should respect the dignity and seriousness of the proceeding, and individuals 
will be restricted to speaking once. Obscene, truly threatening, or overly repetitive comments will be deemed out of order 
and will be interrupted and removed. Topics that are considered out of order also include matters that are in litigation, 
individual employees or employee groups discussing matters for which complaint or grievance procedures are in place, 
personal disputes between the speaker and another resident not germane to City business, support for or opposition to any 
candidate for political office, and personnel complaints pertaining to individual City employees. There is a time limit of 
three minutes per speaker, and the total time allowed for general public comment regarding City business will be limited to 
no more than one hour. The public comment period is for City Council members to listen and not to respond or debate 
with persons. If you do not live in Bangor or own property in Bangor, please allow those who do to have the opportunity to 
speak first. If you’d like to offer comment on any item directly related to City business not appearing on the regular 
agenda, you may approach the podium. Individuals who have appropriately pre-registered to give public comment via 
remote means will be given the opportunity to participate remotely. Alternatively, Councilors may be reached via email 
at councilors@bangormaine.gov. (A link to the adopted public comment policy can be found on the City’s website.)

26-300 ORDER Appointing Grace Innis as Interim City Solicitor FALOON 
    
Executive Summary: This Order will appoint Grace Innis as Interim City Solicitor beginning November 
10, 2026. Under the terms of her employment agreement, Ms. Innis agrees to serve in the capacity of 
Interim City Solicitor, maintain a stable environment and operations of the Legal Department, as well as 
provide continuity on all ongoing items. Council agrees that no new directives requiring considerable 
effort by the Legal Department will be initiated unless they are necessary to carry out the above. Should 
the Council desire to appoint a different Interim Solicitor, or hire a different permanent Solicitor, Ms. Innis 
agrees to resume the duties of Assistant City Solicitor. In recognition of extra duties, Ms. Innis will be 
compensated on the Executive Scale.  
 
Ms. Innis has a Bachelor of Science in Political Science from Texas Woman's University and a Juris 
Doctor from Penn State Law School. She began her career as the Assistant City Solicitor for the City of 
Bangor three years ago. During her time as the Assistant City Solicitor, she has been responsible for 
negotiating a large number of contracts and leases, providing legal guidance to all City departments, 
guiding the Planning Board and other City boards, committees, and commissions as necessary, amending 
policies as directed, and prosecuting a number of ordinance and state law violations. Ms. Innis also serves 
as the City's Public Access Officer, coordinating public records requests across the City, and the City's 
Americans with Disabilities Act Coordinator. 
 
Ms. Innis is admitted to practice before the Courts of the State of Maine and the U.S. District Court for the 
District of Maine. She also sits on the board of the Penobscot County Bar Association.

Executive Summary: This Ordinance amendment would remove Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from the Downtown 
Development District (DDD) to provide flexibility for growth in downtown and promote infill development. 
Floor area ratio is the floor area of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. 
 
FAR was used to control building bulk and volume in the early to mid-20th century. When FARs were 
implemented around the country, some of the perceived benefits were protecting sunlight, neighborhood 
character, and infrastructure capacity, most of which do not hold true today. Additionally, some of the most 
well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For example, the Graham Building where 
the Rudman Winchell offices are located have a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the Eastern Trust building at 6 
State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
 
The proposed amendments align with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations. This item was reviewed and unanimously recommended for approval at the 
Planning Board meeting on October 20, 2026. 
    
26-294 RESOLVE Accepting and Appropriating $823,851 for the Nourish 
ME Rural Nutrition Education Program From the 
University of New England  
DEANE 
    
Executive Summary: This Resolve will accept and appropriate $823,851 from the University of New 
England (UNE) to implement the Nourish ME nutrition education program in fiscal years 2027 and 2028 
in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties. 
 
Maine's Rural Health Transformation Program provides the funds for the Nourish ME program statewide, 
which focuses on reducing the burden of chronic illness through nutrition. Bangor Public Health and 
Community Services implemented SNAP Ed programming from 2012 - 2025. Federal funding for the 
SNAP Education program was ended nationally on February 28, 2026. In response, Maine DHHS 
dedicated new federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding to nutrition education. UNE is the 
implementing agency for the program.  
 
Funding is for a five-year program with year one funding beginning May 1, 2026. This funding allows an 
important program to continue operating despite the loss of federal funding.  In FY25, Bangor Public 
Health and Community Services SNAP Ed nutrition educators provided nutrition education to 3,057 youth 
in 25 schools, and 266 adults in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties. The program helped teach participants 
how to stretch food dollars and make healthy choices.  
 
As a result of this program, statewide:  
 
45% of adults increased eating vegetables  
27% of adults increased use of a grocery list  
53% of teens increased use of nutrition facts labels  
17% of youth increased physical activity 
 
This item was reviewed and unanimously recommended for approval at the Government Operations 
Committee meeting on October 5, 2026.

26-295 RESOLVE Accepting and Appropriating Up to $6,000 from Johns 
Hopkins University as Partners on a National Institutes 
for Health ARISE Grant to Increase Access to PrEP  
WALKER 
    
Executive Summary: This Order will accept and appropriate up to $6,000 from Johns Hopkins University 
as partners on a National Institutes for Health (NIH) ARISE grant to increase access to PrEP. 
 
For the past year, Bangor Public Health and Community Services has been exploring opportunities to expand 
access to Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP). PrEP is an effective medication to prevent the transmission of HIV. 
The current HIV outbreak has revealed gaps in access to PrEP. It is often not offered through traditional 
primary care. As a result, other delivery models need to be established. Bangor Public Health and Community 
Services currently has two clinic locations that could offer PrEP services. In addition to meeting a community 
need, this would also be a billable service to contribute to the Department's revenue. The NIH ARISE grant will 
bring together Johns Hopkins University's expertise and leadership with Bangor Public Health and Community 
Service's on the ground experience to create a plan to include increase access to PrEP through community 
partnerships and system building. The funding will be used to offset staff time to work on developing the plan 
and expenses for supporting community meeting logistics.

26-304 ORDER Amending the Schedule of Fees by Adding New 
Planning Fees Starting November 2, 2026 
FISH 
    
Executive Summary: This Order will amend the City's Schedule of Fees to create two new fees for 
Planning services beginning November 5, 2026. Currently, there is no fee to send mailed notices for land 
development, zone change, or historic preservation applications. However, notices to abutting property 
owners are required for almost all types of development, all zoning map changes, and historic preservation 
applications. Depending on whether the project is a conditional use or there are many abutting property 
owners, mailings can be quite large. Therefore, similar to how the City charges developers for the cost to 
advertise certain developments and review land development permits, staff proposes to charge for the cost 
to mail notices to abutters so that this cost doesn’t fall on taxpayers. 
 
Additionally, the City was given delegated authority by the State to review stormwater permits triggered 
by developments that create 20,000 square feet of new impervious area within an urban impaired stream 
watershed or one acre of impervious area in unimpaired watersheds. However, this authority comes with 
extra staff time needed to review projects and inspect stormwater systems to ensure compliance. The State 
currently charges developers for this permitting; therefore, this new proposed fee would charge similar 
amount for the City to do this permitting. This fee would be charged as part of the land development 
permit application for a project (if it meets the threshold for requiring this permitting), and the stormwater 
permitting portion would be transferred to the Stormwater Utility fund to cover these extra costs. 
 
This item was received and recommended for approval at the October 5, 2026 Business & Economic 
Development Committee meeting.

provide services at The Well to link people to housing, healthcare, and other resources. Last year The Well 
served approximately 70-80 people a day.

26-306 ORDER Finding Councilor Wayne Mallar Violated Two 
Provisions of the City's Ethics Code During a Break at 
the March 31, 2026 Meeting of the City's Ethics Board, 
and Imposing a Requirement to Undergo Training 
FALOON 
    
Executive Summary: This Order would find that Councilor Wayne Mallar's conduct at the March 31, 
2026, Board of Ethics meeting violated two provisions of the City's Ethics Code, and would impose a 
requirement that Councilor Mallar undergo a customized, interactive training program facilitated by Cross 
Cultural Community Services. 
 
While attending the March 31, 2026 Ethics Board meeting and during a break for an executive session, 
Councilor Mallar made the following comments to a City employee in Council Chambers, which were 
picked up by a live microphone and broadcast live to the public on the meeting's YouTube feed: "The 
School Department's asking for a 10% increase.  As far as I'm concerned, they get no increase.  They can't 
speak English, read English or write English.  It's not a disability.  We do not have to furnish.  They're 
probably all illegals anyway.  That's what the cultural center is supposed to be doing." 
 
Bangor schools are required by state and federal law to provide English instruction to multilingual 
students, and failing to fund any such program would violate the law. 
 
Section 33-1 of the Ethics Code requires City Councilors to be fair, impartial and responsive to the needs 
of the people and to maintain a standard of conduct that will inspire public confidence in the integrity of 
the City's government.  Section 33-5.1 of the Ethics Code requires that City Councilors conduct 
themselves in a manner that does not discriminate unlawfully against any person because of race, national 
origin, or cultural group, among other factors. 
 
Upon referral by the City Council, this matter was investigated and reviewed by the City's Board of Ethics, 
and the Board made findings and submitted a written advisory opinion to the Council.  This order follows 
the findings and recommendations made by the Ethics Board, including findings that Councilor Mallar's  
actions violated Sections 33-1 and 33-5.1 of the Ethics Code.  This order also follows the Ethics Board's 
finding that Councilor Mallar's actions did not violate Sec. 33-13.1 of the Ethics Code.

Floor Area Ratio from the Downtown Development District  
 
Summary 
 
This Ordinance amendment would remove Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from the Downtown Development District 
(DDD) to provide flexibility for growth in downtown and promote infill development. Floor area ratio is the 
floor area of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. 
 
FAR was used to control building bulk and volume in the early to mid-20th century. When FARs were 
implemented around the country, some of the perceived benefits were protecting sunlight, neighborhood 
character, and infrastructure capacity, most of which do not hold true today. Additionally, some of the most 
well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For example, the Graham Building 
where the Rudman Winchell offices are located have a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the Eastern Trust 
building at 6 State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
 
The proposed amendments align with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations.

Please accept this memorandum as the recommendation from the Planning Board for the noted item. 
The Commission considered this item in a noticed public hearing on October 20, 2026.   
 
The meeting was conducted in the Council Chambers at City Hall and on Zoom. Members in 
attendance in the Chambers were Chair Jonathan Boucher, Vice Chair Janet Jonas, and Members

used to protect sunlight, neighborhood character, and control building form and bulk. The 
numerous historic districts and façade district that cover most of downtown currently help 
retain neighborhood character and control building form. Additionally, FAR is preventing infill 
development downtown for residential and commercial developments. Staff find that this 
amendment aligns with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply 
downtown by revising zoning regulations. 
 
B. After the workshops with Council and Planning Board, staff discussed with the Fire Department 
and Airport if a maximum height would be needed Downtown. The Fire Department did not 
have concerns with fire response for taller buildings and downtown is outside of the area 
around the airport that would need height restrictions.

ARTICIPATION POLICY 
Pursuant to Title 1, Section 403-B of the Maine Revised Statutes (Section 403-B), and after public 
notice and a hearing, the Bangor City Council hereby adopts the following policy to govern the 
participation, via remote methods, in all public proceedings or meetings of the City of Bangor.  
I. BACKGROUND
The City has 
several public bodies that are subject to the public meetings laws of the Maine Revised 
Statutes (Title 1, Chapter 13 of those statutes) . Those public bodies include boards, commissions, 
and committees as well as the City Council. Generally, the public bodies can be separated into three 
categories, which are as follows: (A) those with final decision-making authority, (B) advisory 
committees, and (C) subcommittees or working gr oups. This Policy will set the guidelines for 
Bangor’s remote participation according to those three categories of meetings.  
The purpose of this Policy is to further participation in meetings and balance said participation with 
staffing concerns.   
II. LEGAL AUTHORITY
Title 1 M.R.S. Section 403-B was adopted on June 1, 2021 by emerge ncy and thus became 
immediately effective. This statute generally allows for remote participation by board members and 
remote attendance by the public in City proceedings, and a recent amendment to the statute allows 
members of a public body to attend remotely in circumstances that can be decided by the body 
itself.  
This Policy will guide when members of the public may participate in proceedings remotely in City 
proceedings and when members of the public body may do the same. It is intended to comply with 
Section 403-B.   
III. POSSIBLE MEANS OF REMOTE PARTICIPATION
Remote methods of participation may incl ude telephonic or video technology allowing 
simultaneous reception of information and may include other means necessary to accommodate 
persons with disabilities.  Should a member of the public require a reasonable accommodation to 
participate by remote means under the Americans with Disabilities Act, please contact the City’s 
ADA Coordinator. Information about accessibility and accommodations can be found at 
https://www.bangormaine.gov/212/Accessibility-Accommodations. Remote participation will not 
be allowed by text-only means, such as e-mail, text messages, or chat functions. 
When available (as detailed below), the City w ill use YouTube Live and internet-based meeting 
software (currently Zoom) to offer public participation. YouTube Live is not monitored, and public 
comment is not accepted via remote means, except as a reasonable accommodation under the ADA.

V.  PROCEDURE FOR DETERMINING EMERGENCY OR URGENT ISSUE 
 
The procedure set forth in this Section V is intended to allow the City and its public bodies to meet 
the notice requirements of Section VI below and Section 403-B. By way of background, the City 
typically posts the agendas for its public bodies on the Friday of the week prior to those meetings. 
These agendas, which are posted both online and at City Hall, serve as notice under Title 1, Section 
406 of the Maine Revised Statutes (“Section 406”) and the City Charter.  
 
With the background in mind, the Council Chair, in consultation with the City Manager, shall have 
authority to determine the existence of an emer gency or urgent issue for all public bodies of the 
City. In determining the existence of an emergency or urgent issue, the Council Chair will use the 
following procedures: 
 
1. On the Thursday or Friday prior to any given week, the Council Chair in consultation 
with the City Manager will evaluate and deci de whether any emergency or urgent issue 
that would require public bodies to meet remotely exists. 
 
In deciding whether such an emergency or urgent issue exists, the Council Chair will not 
be limited by the definitions of “civil emerge ncy” contained in the Code of Ordinances 
or State Law. Instead, the Council Chair should apply the generally understood 
definitions of emergency⁴ or urgent issue.⁵ ⁶ 
 
If the Council Chair decides that such an em ergency or urgent issue exists, City bodies 
shall only meet by remote means. 
 
2. If the Council Chair determines that an emerge ncy or urgent issue exists, the Chair in, 
consultation with the City Manager, will ensure that (a) each agenda contains a 
notification to the public that remote pa rticipation will be available and the means

available to hold remote meetings, the Counc il Chair and/or city staff will notify the 
chairs of each of the City’s public bodies that are to hold meetings in the coming week. 
 
In the event of an emergency or urgent issue that arises after the Council Chair has made an initial 
determination that none existed, the following procedure will be used: 
 
The City Manager, a City Councilor, or the chair of any of the City’s public bodies, may 
bring a potential emergency or urgent issue to the Council Chair’s attention. The Council 
Chair, or in the event that a chair of a public body is unable to reach the Council Chair 
after multiple attempts, the chair of said body will then, in consul tation with the City 
Manager or the public body’s assigned city staff, ⁸ determine whether an emergency or 
urgent issue that would require remote meetings exists. If the Council Chair or, when 
applicable, public body chair dete rmines that such an emergency or urgent issue exists, 
the Council Chair or public body chair, in consultation with the City Manager (or 
applicable assigned city staff), will determine (a) if there is time to provide notification 
to the public of the ability to attend the m eeting(s) remotely, and (b) if staffing and 
resources are available to hold a remote meeting or meetings. If there is both time to 
provide notification and staffing and resources are available, the City Manager and other 
city staff will take all steps necessary to ma ke notification of the availability of remote 
participation to the public and members of the affected public bodies. 
 
If the Council Chair or public body chair decides that such an emergency or urgent issue 
exists, the Council Chair or, where applicable , the public body chair, shall also decide 
whether the emergency or urgent issue requires the City public bodies to meet only by 
remote means or if a hybrid meeting may be conducted. 
 
The Council Chair has the discretion to allo w public comment by remote methods if an 
emergency or urgent issue exists, but the Chair is not required to allow public comment 
by remote methods during such times. 
 
A meeting may not be changed to a remote par ticipation only meeting when there is less than 
twenty-four hours available to notify the public.⁹ 
 
VI.  NOTICE 
 
Notice of all meetings will be provided in accordance with Title 1, Section 406 of the Maine 
Revised Statutes, and the City Charter, City Code  or policy, if applicable. When the public may 
attend via remote methods, the notice will incl ude the means by which the public may access the 
meeting remotely and will provide a method for disabled persons to request necessary 
accommodation to access the meeting. Notice will also identify the location where the public may 
attend the meeting in person. The public body will  not restrict in person, public attendance to 
meetings except in the case of an emergency or urgent issue that requires it to meet using only 
remote methods of attendance.

Amending the Schedule of Fees by Adding New Planning Fees Starting November 5, 2026
This Order will amend the City's Schedule of Fees to create two new fees for Planning services 
beginning November 5, 2026. Currently, there is no fee to send mailed notices for land development, 
zone change, or historic preservation applications. However, notices to abutting property owners are 
required for almost all types of development, all zoning map changes, and historic preservation 
applications. Depending on whether the project is a conditional use or there are many abutting 
property owners, mailings can be quite large. Therefore, similar to how the City charges developers for 
the cost to advertise certain developments and review land development permits, staff proposes to 
charge for the cost to mail notices to abutters so that this cost doesn’t fall on taxpayers. 
 
Additionally, the City was given delegated authority by the State to review stormwater permits 
triggered by developments that create 20,000 square feet of new impervious area within an urban 
impaired stream watershed or one acre of impervious area in unimpaired watersheds. However, this 
authority comes with extra staff time needed to review projects and inspect stormwater systems to 
ensure compliance. The State currently charges developers for this permitting; therefore, this new 
proposed fee would charge similar amount for the City to do this permitting. This fee would be charged 
as part of the land development permit application for a project (if it meets the threshold for requiring 
this permitting), and the stormwater permitting portion would be transferred to the Stormwater Utility 
fund to cover these extra costs. 
 
This item was received and recommended for approval at the October 5, 2026 Business & Economic 
Development Committee meeting.

Authorizing the City Manager to Direct up to $105,000 from Bangor Community Development Block Grant to 
Bangor Public Health and Community Services to Fund Three Non-Profit Organizations
This Order will authorize the City Manager to direct up to $105,000 from Bangor Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) to 
Bangor Public Health and Community Services to fund three non-profit organizations. This item requires a public hearing prior to 
voting.
 
Contingent upon eligibility, the Manna will receive up to $5,000 to rehabilitate their damaged kitchen. The Manna provides a warm 
meal daily for anyone in the community. The Well will receive $10,000 to support their operations of a warming day space. The Well 
operates a day space that offers a safe place for people to be during the day as well as food, clothing, phone charging, and laundry 
services. A number of programs such as OPTIONS team, PCHC street outreach, City outreach, PATH, and other organizations provide 
services at The Well to link people to housing, healthcare, and other resources. Last year The Well served approximately 70-80 people 
a day.
 
Up to $90,000 will be allocated to support an as-needed warming overnight shelter particularly on cold nights when demand is 
expected to be highest between November 2026 and April 2027. Based upon their experience coordinating a warming shelter during 
the 2025-2026 winter, Together Place is best situated to receive the funding. The proposed funding sources for the as-needed 
warming shelter include heating assistance funding administered by Public Health and Community Services ($5,000), General 
Assistance reimbursement (approximately $11,000), and Community Development Block Grant ($90,000). The Advisory Committee on 
Homelessness will assist by developing requirements and policy for operating the as-needed warming shelter. The funding will reflect 
actual costs and expenses.
 
This order further authorizes the Director of Public Health and Community Services and the Community Development Officer to execute
 any and all documents to effectuate this Award. These awards will be subject to further eligibility. The Director of Public Health and 
Community Services and the Community Development Officer will develop routine reporting requirements.

Finding Councilor Wayne Mallar Violated Two Provisions of the City's Ethics Code During a Break at the March 
31, 2026 Meeting of the City's Ethics Board, and Imposing a Requirement to Undergo Training 
This Order would find that Councilor Wayne Mallar's conduct at the March 31, 2026, Board of Ethics meeting violated two provisions of the City's Ethics Code, and would 
impose a requirement that Councilor Mallar undergo a customized, interactive training program facilitated by Cross Cultural Community Services.
While attending the March 31, 2026 Ethics Board meeting and during a break for an executive session, Councilor Mallar made the following comments to a City employee in 
Council Chambers, which were picked up by a live microphone and broadcast live to the public on the meeting's YouTube feed: "The School Department's asking for a 10% 
increase.  As far as I'm concerned, they get no increase.  They can't speak English, read English or write English.  It's not a disability.  We do not have to furnish.  They're 
probably all illegals anyway.  That's what the cultural center is supposed to be doing."
Bangor schools are required by state and federal law to provide English instruction to multilingual students, and failing to fund any such program would violate the law.
Section 33-1 of the Ethics Code requires City Councilors to be fair, impartial and responsive to the needs of the people and to maintain a standard of conduct that will inspire 
public confidence in the integrity of the City's government.  Section 33-5.1 of the Ethics Code requires that City Councilors conduct themselves in a manner that does not 
discriminate unlawfully against any person because of race, national origin, or cultural group, among other factors.
Upon referral by the City Council, this matter was investigated and reviewed by the City's Board of Ethics, and the Board made findings and submitted a written advisory 
opinion to the Council.  This order follows the findings and recommendations made by the Ethics Board, including findings that Councilor Mallar's actions violated Sections 
33-1 and 33-5.1 of the Ethics Code.  This order also follows the Ethics Board's finding that Councilor Mallar's actions did not violate Sec. 33-13.1 of the Ethics Code.
Upon return of this matter from the Ethics Board, the Council requested a recommendation from the City's Advisory Committee on Racial Equity, Inclusion and Human Rights 
("ACREIHR") on appropriate training.  This order adopts the first recommendation made by ACREIHR--for customized, interactive training facilitated by Cross Cultural 
Community Services ("CCCS"), a Maine-based organization specializing in cultural competency, equity, and inclusive practices.  CCCS offers tailored educational programs that
 encourage participants to examine personal assumptions, recognize the influence of bias, and develop skills for respectful engagement across cultural differences.

Finding Councilor Wayne Mallar Violated Two Provisions of the City's Ethics Code During a Break at the March 
31, 2026 Meeting of the City's Ethics Board, and Imposing a Requirement to Undergo Training 
WHEREAS, during a recess of a March 31, 2026 meeting of the City's Ethics Board, City Councilor Wayne 
Mallar made the following remarks to a City staff member in Council Chambers which were picked up by a 
microphone and broadcast on the meeting's live YouTube feed: "The School Department's asking for a 10% 
increase.  As far as I'm concerned, they get no increase.  They can't speak English, read English or write 
English.  It's not a disability.  We do not have to furnish.  They're probably all illegals anyway.  That's what 
the cultural center is supposed to be doing."; and   
WHEREAS, Bangor schools are required by state and federal law to provide English instruction to multilingual 
students, and 
    
WHEREAS, by Council Order 26-152, this Council referred to the City's Ethics Board for investigation, findings, 
and an advisory opinion the issues of whether Councilor Mallar's actions violated certain provisions of the 
City's Ethics Code; and 
WHEREAS, the Ethics Board investigated, held public hearing, deliberated, made findings, and approved and 
submitted a written Advisory Opinion on the referred issues; and 
WHEREAS, this Council wishes to follow the findings and recommendations made by the Ethics Board; and 
WHEREAS, this Council requested a recommendation from the City's Advisory Committee on Racial Equity, 
Inclusion, and Human Rights ("ACREIHR") on appropriate training, and ACREIHR's first recommendation was 
for customized, interactive training facilitated by Cross Cultural Community Services; and  
WHEREAS, this Council wishes to adopt the first recommendation made by ACREIHR.     
Be it Ordered by the City Council of the City of Bangor that, the City Council hereby adopts the Ethics Board's 
findings that on March 31, 2026 during a recess of the City's Ethics Board meeting, Councilor Wayne Mallar 
made the above-quoted comments to a City staff member in Council Chambers, which comments were picked 
up by a live microphone and broadcast to the public on the meeting's live YouTube feed. 
The Council adopts the Ethics Board's findings that Councilor Mallar's actions violated (1) Sec. 33-1 of the 
City's Ethics Code, which requires that City Councilors be fair, impartial and responsive to the needs of the 
people and maintain a standard of conduct that will inspire public confidence in the integrity of the City's 
government; and (2) Sec. 33-5.1 of the Ethics Code, which requires City Councilors to conduct themselves in
a manner that does not discriminate unlawfully against any person because of race, national origin, or 
cultural group.  The Council also adopts the Ethics Board's finding that Councilor Mallar's actions did not 
violate Sec. 33-13.1 of the Ethics Code. 
The Council also adopts the first recommendation of the City’s Advisory Committee on Racial Equity, 
Inclusion, and Human Rights and, pursuant to §33-23(B)(3)(e) of the City’s Ethics Code, orders Councilor 
Mallar to complete within a reasonable time a customized, interactive training session facilitated by 
Cross Cultural Community Services that encourages participants to examine personal assumptions, 
recognize the influence of bias, and develop skills for respectful engagement across cultural differences.
